transcription.tex: \textbf{Mathematics · Mechanics Year 2}\par Chapter 5\par \textbf{Forces and friction}\par Resolving forces · Inclined planes · Limiting friction

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Resolving forces}\par Replace a force by perpendicular components. Use these to find a resultant or apply Newton’s second law.

\textbf{Inclined planes}\par Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane.\par \textbf{Friction}\par Distinguish friction below its limiting value from limiting friction.\par Unless stated otherwise, use \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A displacement of \(5\,\mathrm m\) makes \(60^\circ\) above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.
\[x=5\cos60^\circ=2.5\,\mathrm m,\]\[y=5\sin60^\circ=4.33\,\mathrm m.\]
A force of \(7\,\mathrm N\) makes \(60^\circ\) to the upward vertical, towards the right. Resolve it.
\[F_x=7\sin60^\circ=6.06\,\mathrm N,\]\[F_y=7\cos60^\circ=3.5\,\mathrm N.\]
\textbf{Tip:} the component adjacent to the stated angle uses cosine; the opposite component uses sine.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Resolve \(8\,\mathrm N\), \(30^\circ\) above the positive horizontal.
\[4\sqrt3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j\ \mathrm N.\]
Resolve \(6\,\mathrm N\), \(45^\circ\) above the negative horizontal.
\[-3\sqrt2\mathbf i+3\sqrt2\mathbf j\ \mathrm N.\]
Resolve \(9\,\mathrm N\), \(37^\circ\) below the positive horizontal.
\[7.19\mathbf i-5.42\mathbf j\ \mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A box of mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) rests on a smooth horizontal floor. A force of \(10\,\mathrm N\) pulls at \(30^\circ\) above the horizontal. Find the acceleration and normal reaction.
Horizontal:\[8a=10\cos30^\circ\Rightarrow a=\frac{5\sqrt3}{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]\par Vertical equilibrium:\[R+10\sin30^\circ=8g\]\[\Rightarrow R=8g-5=73.4\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Find the resultant of \(10\,\mathrm N\) at \(45^\circ\) above the positive horizontal and \(8\,\mathrm N\) at \(30^\circ\) below it.

\[F_x=10\cos45^\circ+8\cos30^\circ=13.999,\]\[F_y=10\sin45^\circ-8\sin30^\circ=3.071.\]\[|\mathbf F|=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}=14.3\,\mathrm N.\]\[\theta=\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)=12.4^\circ\]\par above the positive horizontal.\par Alternatively, use the cosine rule with the \(105^\circ\) internal angle of the force triangle, then the sine rule.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Find the resultant of \(3\,\mathrm N\), \(25^\circ\) left of the upward vertical, and \(4\,\mathrm N\), \(32^\circ\) below the positive horizontal.
\[F_x=4\cos32^\circ-3\sin25^\circ=2.124,\]\[F_y=3\cos25^\circ-4\sin32^\circ=0.599.\]\[|\mathbf F|=2.21\,\mathrm N,\quad\theta=15.8^\circ\]\par above the positive horizontal.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5A · Question 4}\par Three forces are in equilibrium. Angles below are measured anticlockwise from the positive horizontal. Find the magnitude and direction of \(B\).\par (a) \(15\,\mathrm N\) at \(150^\circ\); \(20\,\mathrm N\) at \(210^\circ\).
\[B_x=35\cos30^\circ,\quad B_y=5\sin30^\circ.\]\[B=30.4\,\mathrm N,\quad\theta=4.72^\circ\]\par above the positive horizontal.
(b) \(25\,\mathrm N\) at \(50^\circ\); \(10\,\mathrm N\) at \(-30^\circ\).
\[B_x=-25\cos50^\circ-10\cos30^\circ,\]\[B_y=-25\sin50^\circ+10\sin30^\circ.\]\[B=28.5\,\mathrm N,\quad\theta=29.8^\circ\]\par below the negative horizontal.
(c) \(10\,\mathrm N\) at \(120^\circ\); \(20\,\mathrm N\) at \(-20^\circ\).
\[B_x=5-20\cos20^\circ,\]\[B_y=-10\sin60^\circ+20\sin20^\circ.\]\[B=13.9\,\mathrm N,\quad\theta=7.52^\circ\]\par below the negative horizontal.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5A · Question 6}\par A \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle on a smooth horizontal surface is pulled by \(P\) at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal. Its acceleration is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find \(P\). (3 marks)
\[P\cos45^\circ=10(2)\]\[\Rightarrow P=20\sqrt2\,\mathrm N.\]

\textbf{Question 7}\par A particle of mass \(m\) on a smooth horizontal surface is pulled by \(20\,\mathrm N\) at \(25^\circ\) above the horizontal. Its acceleration is \(0.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find \(m\). (3 marks)
\[20\cos25^\circ=0.5m\]\[\Rightarrow m=40\cos25^\circ=36.3\,\mathrm{kg}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5A · Question 8}\par A parachutist of mass \(80\,\mathrm{kg}\) descends at constant velocity. Two supporting lines each make \(60^\circ\) with the horizontal and have tension \(T\). Air resistance on the parachutist is one quarter of the weight. Find \(T\).
Air resistance is \(20g\,\mathrm N\) upwards.\par Vertical equilibrium gives\[2T\sin60^\circ+20g=80g.\]\[T=\frac{60g}{2\sin60^\circ}=20\sqrt3g\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5A · Question 9}\par Forces act at a point: \(12\,\mathrm N\) vertically upwards, \(F_1\) horizontally right, and \(F_2\) at \(30^\circ\) below the negative horizontal. Their resultant is \((2\sqrt3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N\). Find \(F_1,F_2\).
Vertical components:\[12-F_2\sin30^\circ=2\Rightarrow F_2=20\,\mathrm N.\]\par Horizontal components:\[F_1-20\cos30^\circ=2\sqrt3\]\[\Rightarrow F_1=12\sqrt3\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A particle of mass \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) slides down a smooth plane inclined at \(15^\circ\). Find the normal reaction and acceleration.

Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane.\par Perpendicular equilibrium:\[R=10g\cos15^\circ=94.7\,\mathrm N.\]\par Down the plane:\[10g\sin15^\circ=10a\]\[\Rightarrow a=g\sin15^\circ=2.54\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

slides.title: Inclined Plane with an additional force

transcription.tex: A particle of mass \(m\) is pushed up a smooth \(30^\circ\) slope by a force of \(5g\,\mathrm N\). The force makes \(60^\circ\) with the upward slope, directed into the plane. The acceleration is \(0.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) up the slope. Find \(m\).
Resolve up the slope:\[5g\cos60^\circ-mg\sin30^\circ=0.5m.\]\[5g-mg=m\]\[\Rightarrow m=\frac{5g}{1+g}=4.54\,\mathrm{kg}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle on a smooth plane is pulled by \(4\,\mathrm N\) up the plane. The inclination \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). Find the acceleration.
Using a \(3,4,5\) triangle, \(\sin\alpha=3/5\).\par Taking up the slope as positive:\[4-2g\frac35=2a\Rightarrow a=-3.88.\]\par The acceleration is \(3.88\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) down the slope.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5B · Question 4}\par A \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle is pulled up a rough \(15^\circ\) slope by a \(30\,\mathrm N\) force parallel to the plane, at constant velocity.\par (a) Draw a force diagram. (4 marks)\par (b) Find the frictional force. (5 marks)

(a) Weight \(6g\) vertically down; reaction perpendicular out of the plane; \(30\,\mathrm N\) up the plane; friction \(F\) down the plane.\par (b) Up the plane:\[30-6g\sin15^\circ-F=0\]\[F=30-6g\sin15^\circ=14.8\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5B · Question 5}\par A particle of mass \(m\) slides down a smooth \(30^\circ\) plane. The normal reaction is \(5\,\mathrm N\). Find (a) \(m\) (3 marks); (b) its acceleration (3 marks).
(a) \[mg\cos30^\circ=5\]\[m=\frac5{g\cos30^\circ}=0.589\,\mathrm{kg}.\]\par (b) \[mg\sin30^\circ=ma\]\[a=g\sin30^\circ=4.9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\]\par down the slope.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5B · Question 6}\par A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle on a smooth \(30^\circ\) slope is pushed by a horizontal \(30\,\mathrm N\) force towards the rising slope. Find its acceleration.
The component of the applied force up the slope is \(30\cos30^\circ\).\[30\cos30^\circ-5g\sin30^\circ=5a\]\[a=0.296\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\]\par up the slope.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5B · Question 7}\par A \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle on a rough \(40^\circ\) slope has a vertically upward force of \(6\,\mathrm N\) applied. It moves at constant velocity. Find the frictional force.
The resultant of weight and the applied vertical force is \((3g-6)\,\mathrm N\) downwards. Friction acts up the slope.\[F=(3g-6)\sin40^\circ\]\[F=15.0\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5B · Question 8}\par A particle of mass \(m\) moves up a rough slope with \(\tan\alpha=1/\sqrt3\). A \(26\,\mathrm N\) force acts \(45^\circ\) above the plane. Friction is \(12\,\mathrm N\) down the plane and the acceleration is \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) up the plane. Find \(m\) to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
\(\alpha=30^\circ\). Resolving up the plane:\[26\cos45^\circ-12-mg\sin30^\circ=m.\]\[m=\frac{13\sqrt2-12}{1+g/2}=1.08\,\mathrm{kg}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Friction adjusts to the situation}\par 1. No horizontal force on a stationary object on a horizontal surface: \(F=0\).\par 2. Pull \(T\) on a stationary object: friction balances \(T\), until the limiting value is reached.

3. At limiting equilibrium, or sliding in the model used here:\[F=\mu R.\]\par Friction opposes motion, or the tendency to move.\par Below the limit:\[0\le F\le\mu R.\]\par Do not automatically use \(F=\mu R\) for every stationary particle.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Coefficient of friction}\[F_{\max}=\mu R.\]\par \(\mu\) is dimensionless and describes the pair of surfaces.\par \(R\) is the normal reaction, not automatically the weight.

Rougher surfaces generally have a larger coefficient. A larger normal reaction increases the limiting friction.\par On an inclined plane, resolve perpendicular to the plane first. Applied forces can change \(R\).\par \(\mu\) need not be less than 1.

\textbf{Illustrative static coefficients from the source}\par Steel on steel: 0.74; aluminium on steel: 0.61.\par Copper on steel: 0.53; rubber on concrete: 1.0.\par Wood on wood: 0.25–0.5; glass on glass: 0.94.\par Waxed wood on wet snow: 0.14.\par Ice on ice: 0.10; Teflon on Teflon: 0.04.\par Synovial joints: 0.01.\par No value was supplied for waxed wood on dry snow or lubricated metal on metal.

transcription.tex: A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle slides down a rough \(30^\circ\) plane with acceleration \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find \(\mu\).
\[R=2g\cos30^\circ.\]\par Down the plane:\[2g\sin30^\circ-\mu R=2(1).\]\[\mu=\frac{g-2}{2g\cos30^\circ}=0.460.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel M1 June 2013 · Question 3}\par A box of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) rests on a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\). A light inextensible rope pulls at angle \(\alpha\) above the plane, where \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). The coefficient of friction is \(1/3\). The box is on the point of moving up the plane. Model it as a particle and find the tension. (8 marks)

\(\sin\alpha=3/5,\ \cos\alpha=4/5\).\par Perpendicular to the plane:\[R+\frac35T=2g\cos30^\circ.\]\par Friction is \(R/3\) down the plane:\[\frac45T-\frac R3=2g\sin30^\circ.\]\par Substitute for \(R\):\[T=g\left(1+\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)=15.5\,\mathrm N.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5C · Question 6}\par A sled of mass \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) is pulled across rough horizontal ground by a force \(P\) at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal towards the left. Given \(\mu=0.1\) and acceleration \(0.3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) left, find \(P\).
\[R+P\sin45^\circ=10g.\]\par Resolving left:\[P\cos45^\circ-0.1R=10(0.3).\]\[P(\cos45^\circ+0.1\sin45^\circ)=3+g.\]\[P=16.5\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5C · Question 7}\par A train travelling at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) stops in \(30\,\mathrm s\) after its wheels lock.\par (a) Model the train as a particle and assume friction is the only resistance. Find \(\mu\).
\[a=\frac{0-20}{30}=-\frac23\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]\[R=mg,\quad-\mu mg=-\frac23m\]\[\Rightarrow\mu=\frac2{3g}=0.0680.\]
(b) How would allowing for air resistance change the inferred coefficient? (2 marks)

It would decrease. Air resistance also contributes to the observed deceleration, so less friction is required.\par With air resistance \(A\):\[\mu mg+A=\frac23m\]\[\Rightarrow\mu=\frac2{3g}-\frac A{mg}.\]

transcription.tex: A particle is on the point of sliding down a rough plane inclined at \(\theta\). Prove that \(\mu=\tan\theta\). Can \(\mu\) exceed 1?
\[R=mg\cos\theta.\]\par Limiting equilibrium along the plane:\[mg\sin\theta=\mu R=\mu mg\cos\theta.\]\[\boxed{\mu=\tan\theta}.\]\par Yes: when \(\theta>45^\circ\), \(\tan\theta>1\).
